newsitem.title: UKRAINE: FEATURE - Ukraine's Sevastopol port hoping for better future.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Ukraine's Sevastopol port hoping for better future.

text.p: Smashed to smithereens twice in 100 years, passed like a parcel from Moscow to Kiev by Nikita Khrushchev and now a bargaining chip in post-Soviet politics, this Crimean port surely deserves a harmonious 21st century.
Everyone seems to be living in hope in the crumbling naval base founded by Catherine the Great in 1783 but ceded with the rest of the peninsula as a "gift" to Soviet Ukraine in 1954.
Since Ukraine became independent more than five years ago, Sevastopol has been in limbo, its status under question as Moscow and Kiev squabble over its greatest prize -- the Black Sea Fleet.

But a deal sealed by the two countries' prime ministers on Wednesday leasing the port to Russia for 20 years and plans for Russian President Boris Yeltsin to sign a post-Soviet friendship treaty with Kiev on Saturday could end the uncertainty.
Ukrainian naval officers among the population of about half a million said this week they hoped stage two of the Fleet's division would go ahead, increasing their share by 52 vessels.
Members of the quarter of the population which is Ukrainian said they were hoping the number of schools where classes are taught in Ukrainian would increase from one at present.
Meanwhile the two-thirds Russian majority is wondering if it backed the right horse by supporting Ukrainian independence in 1991 as economic problems abound.

But settling the Fleet's status could pull investors into their city. "International financial organisations say we will only get an investment programme once the question of the Fleet is settled," Sergei Vlasenko, deputy head of the port's administration for economic issues, said.

Parliamentarians are hoping President Leonid Kuchma will stop overturning their decisions, reminding them Crimea's autonomy is limited by the constitution approved last June. Some rue the day they cancelled plans for an independence referendum.
Hoping hardest of all are devotees of the once mighty Black Sea Fleet, who have watched more than 200 years of history rotting in the city's bays while politicians argue.
RUSSIAN SHIPS STILL SAILING UNDER SOVIET FLAG

Ships under blue-and-yellow Ukrainian flags and Russian vessels under Soviet flags share moorings at the port, where lines of rotting grey hulks are testament to economic problems in Moscow and Kiev and doubts about the Fleet's future.
Members of the two navies each declare their sailors have it better. "At least we get paid on time," Deputy Commander Anatoly Vershkov told Reuters on the decks of Ukraine's Slavutych.
"Most of the ones who moved to the Ukrainian side want to come back now, they get paid so little," a Russian officer said.
Andrei Grachev, head of the Russian Fleet's press service, was in a bitter mood ahead of Yeltsin's visit to Kiev this week.
"Formally we have not belonged to any state for five and a half years. For us it has been very tough, above all psychologically. People are tired," he said.
Even Grachev's opposite number and arch-rival in the smaller Ukrainian share of the Fleet agreed. "It's absurd," he said of the ships lined up under the Soviet hammer and sickle.

And Grachev, whose mood blackened as he faced up to the unglorious end of the Soviet Fleet, said he was counting on time healing a tendency among Ukrainian politicians to seek the withdrawal of a foreign military force from their land.
"In 20 years a new generation of politicians will come who might think differently. It's quite possible they will not think about how to evict the fleet of a brotherly state," he said.
"We have hopes," is all he would say of Yeltsin's visit to Ukraine.

Sevastopol's defence is an emotional issue for former Soviet sailors, especially when they recall that a 250-day Nazi siege in 1942 and 349 days of bombardment by British, French and Turkish forces in the 19th century devastated the city.
RUSSIAN MAJORITY SUFFERING IDENTITY CRISIS
Settling the Fleet issue may calm troubled political relations between the two most powerful former Soviet states, but it is unlikely to heal the Crimean Russians' identity crisis.
Like the industrial east of Ukraine, Crimea is almost exclusively Russian-speaking, and a reduction in Russian language broadcasts recently brought a howl of protest.

The Fleet is the symbol of their identity, and now it is divided. "It's very painful," said Albina, 65, as she waited to boost her $25 a month pension by showing tourists round the St Vladimir Cathedral.
"Nothing good will come of it. Sevastopol and the Fleet are synonymous. One has never existed without the other," she said.
For Genya Kruglov, a fiercely pro-Russian deputy in the city council who clearly sees himself as still living in the Soviet Union, only Slav unity will heal the wound.
"But if there's one thing that proves the Russian-ness of Crimea, it's the Prince Vladimir Cathedral standing up on the hill," he railed, missing the irony of his declaration.
Vladimir, or Volodymyr the Great as he is known in Ukraine, founded what eventually became Russian orthodoxy in the 10th century -- when the power centre of Slavonic rule was in Kiev.
